DeepSeek's cheapest model just beat its own flagship on all nine published agent benchmarks - same backbone, same silicon, zero new parameters. The 7.4x jump came from post-training alone. The budget tier just became the frontier.

On July 31, DeepSeek shipped V4-Flash-0731, the official release of its budget coding model. Terminal Bench 2.1 went from 61.8 to 82.7, above the V4-Pro preview's 72.1. DeepSWE, which grades real GitHub issue resolution, jumped 7.3 to 54.4. Price stayed at $0.28 per million output tokens - roughly 1/90th of Claude Opus 4.8, a 99% discount (Axios).

The release inverts the tiering logic the model market is built on. The cheap model is now the better agent than the premium one. That is not naming - it is a claim about where capability actually comes from. DeepSeek squeezed a ~7.4x benchmark gain out of data and training technique on fixed hardware. In an export-control world, that is the one lever that cannot be listed, banned or seized. Compute scarcity does not just force efficiency - it forces a repeatable recipe for converting the same compute into more intelligence. And the recipe is open: MIT license, ungated weights, self-hostable on four A100s.

The US-China twist is the distribution channel. V4-Flash natively supports OpenAI's Responses API and is adapted for Codex - US developers can route agent loops to a Chinese open-weight model inside OpenAI's own tools. A 98% cache-hit discount (industry norm ~90%) is engineered for exactly the long, context-heavy agent sessions that make model choice a bill rather than a brand. OpenAI cut Luna's price 80% the day before and still trails on per-task cost.

The chip war's most effective export is turning out to be a training recipe and an API spec. Washington polices borders; DeepSeek distributes through protocols. Intelligence gets cheaper every week - the open question is who keeps the margin.
